G.142 (V.7): Equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio, as also has the same to equal magnitudes.
G.143 (V.def.4): Magnitudes are said tohave a ratio to one another which are capable, when multiplied, of exceeding one another.

G.145 (V.8): Of unequal magnitudes, the greater has to the same a greater ratio than the less has; and the same has to the less a greater ratio than it has to the greater.
G.146 (V.9): Magnitudes which have the same ratio to the same are equal; and magnitudes to which the same has the same ratio are equal.
G.182 (V.def.9): When three magnitudes are proportional, the first is said to have to the third theduplicate ratio of that which it has to the second.
G.199 (VII.def.12): Numbers prime to one another are those which are measured by an unit alone as a common measure.

G.202 (VII.3): Given three numbers not prime to one another, to find their greatest common measure.
G.203 (VII.4): Any number is either a part or parts of any number, the less of the greater.
G.204 (VII.5): If a number be a part of a number, and another be the same part of another, the sum is the same part of the sum that the one is of the one.
G.205 (VII.6): If a number be parts of a number, and another be the same parts of another, the sum is the same parts of the sum that the one is of the one.

G.210 (VII.def.20): **Numbers** areproportional when the first is the same multiple, or the same part, or the same parts, of the second that the third is of the fourth.
G.212 (VII.12): If there be as many numbers as we please in proportion, then, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents.
G.213 (VII.13): If four numbers be proportional, they is proportional alternately.
G.214 (VII.14): If there be as many numbers as we please, and others equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two are in the same ratio, they is in the same ratio ex aequali.

G.216 (VII.16): If two numbers by multiplying one another make certain numbers, the numbers so produced are equal.
G.217 (VII.17): If a number by multiplying two numbers make certain numbers, the numbers so produced will have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied.
G.218 (VII.18): If two numbers by multiplying any number make certain numbers, the numbers so produced will have the same ratio as the multipliers.

G.220 (VII.20): The least numbers of those which have the same ratio with them measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the greater the greater and the less the less.
G.221 (VII.21): Numbers prime to one another are the least of those which have the same ratio with them.
G.222 (VII.def.15): A number is said tomultiply a number when that which is multiplied is added to itself as many times as there are units in the other, and thus some number is produced.
G.223 (VII.22): The least numbers of those which have the same ratio with them are prime to one another.
G.224 (VII.23): If two numbers be prime to one another, the number which measures the one of them is prime to the remaining number.
G.225 (VII.24): If two numbers be prime to any number, their product also is prime to the same.
G.226 (VII.25): If two numbers be prime to one another, the product of one of them into itself is prime to the remaining one.
G.227 (VII.26): If two numbers be prime to two numbers, both to each, their products also is prime to one another.

G.234 (VII.33): Given as many numbers as we please, to find the least of those which have the same ratio with them.

G.242 (VIII.2): Find numbers in continued proportion, as many as may be prescribed, and the least that are in a given ratio.
G.243 (VIII.3): If as many numbers as we please in continued proportion be the least of those which have the same ratio with them, the extremes of them are prime to one another.
G.246 (VIII.6): If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the first do not measure the second, neither will any other measure any other.
G.247 (VIII.7): If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the first measure the last, it will measure the second also.
G.251 (VIII.11): Between two square numbers there is one mean proportional number, and the square has to the square the ratio duplicate of that which the side has to the side.

G.253 (VIII.12): Between two cube numbers there are two mean proportional numbers, and the cube has to the cube the ratio triplicate of that which the side has to the side.
G.256 (VIII.15): If a cube number measure a cube number, the side will also measure the side; and, if the side measure the side, the cube will also measure the cube.
